title: Investigating Receptor-ligand Systems of the Cellulosome with AFM-based Single-molecule Force Spectroscopy
protocol: Place cover glass in a PTFE holder.
Sonicate cover glass in 1:1 ethanol : ultrapure water (v/v) for 15 min.
Rinse cover glass with ultrapure water.
Place cover glass in piranha solution for 30 min.
Thoroughly rinse cover glass with ultrapure water.
Dry cover glass under a gentle stream of N2.
Submerge cover glass in ethanol, ultrapure water, and 3-aminopropyl dimethyl ethoxysilane mixture at RT for 60 min.
Sequentially submerge cover glass in ethanol and ultrapure water (twice each).
Dry cover glass under a gentle stream of N2.
Bake cover glass in an oven at 80 °C for 30 min.
Place cantilevers on a clean glass slide.
Treat cantilevers with UV-ozone for 15 min.
Submerge cantilevers in ethanol and 3-aminopropyl dimethyl ethoxysilane mixture with ultrapure water catalyst for 3 min.
Rinse cantilevers sequentially in toluene, ethanol, and ultrapure water with gentle stirring.
Dry cantilevers carefully on filter paper between rinses.
Place treated cantilevers on a clean glass slide.
Bake cantilevers at 80 °C for 30 min.
Prepare aliquots of TCEP disulfide reducing beads in micro-tubes.
Cut micropipette tips with scissors to widen the hole diameter when pipetting the TCEP bead slurry.
Rinse TCEP bead slurry with 1 ml TBS buffer and centrifuge at 850 rcf for 3 min.
Carefully remove and discard the supernatant with a micropipette.
Repeat rinsing and discarding steps two more times.
Apply concentrated protein solution (1-10 mg/ml) to the TCEP beads in a ratio of 1:2 (v/v).
Gently mix by stirring with micropipette tip, avoiding air bubbles.
Place protein/TCEP bead slurry mixture on a rotator for 2.5 hr.
Soak aminosilanized cantilevers and cover glasses in sodium borate buffer (pH 8.5) for 45 min to deprotonate primary amine groups on the surface.
Warm NHS-PEG-maleimide powder up to room temperature before opening the cap and weighing.
Store unused NHS-PEG-maleimide under argon at -20 °C.
Apply approximately 30 μl of polymer solution per cantilever, and 90 μl per 2 cover glasses (sandwiched together) for modification with NHS-PEG-maleimide linkers.
Weigh the 5 kDa NHS-PEG-maleimide.
Add sodium borate buffer to obtain a 25 mM solution.
Vortex the mixture.
Incubate cantilevers in 30 µl droplets of NHS-PEG-maleimide solution in a Petri dish.
Place 90 µl of NHS-PEG-maleimide solution onto a single cover glass and add a second cover glass on top to create a sandwich with the solution in between.
Incubate cantilevers/cover glasses with the NHS-PEG-maleimide solution in a water-saturated atmosphere at RT for 1 hr.
Centrifuge TCEP-bead/reduced protein solutions at 100 rcf for 1 min and collect the supernatant.
Dilute the protein solution with TBS to achieve a concentration range of 0.5-2 mg/ml.
Set the reduced and diluted protein solutions aside while rinsing cantilevers and cover glasses.
Rinse cantilevers and cover glasses in three sequential beakers of ultrapure water.
Carefully remove residual liquid from cover glasses by touching the edges to a filter paper under a gentle stream of N2.
Carefully remove residual liquid from cantilevers by touching them to a filter paper.
Apply diluted protein solution immediately.
Mount cover glasses in an appropriate sample holder compatible with the AFM instrument.
Incubate PEGylated cover glasses and cantilevers with respective diluted protein solutions at room temperature for 1-2 hours.
Rinse cantilevers in three sequential beakers with TBS to remove unbound proteins.
Pipette rinse cover glasses at least 10 times.
Store cantilevers and cover glasses under TBS prior to measurement.
Mount the functionalized cantilever and glass surface on the AFM.
Keep the surface covered with buffer throughout the procedure.
Minimize exposure to air when mounting the cantilever.
Adjust the laser beam correctly.
Let the system equilibrate for at least 30 min.
Record a thermal noise spectrum with the cantilever far from the surface.
Use the acoustic approach to find the surface without damaging the cantilever tip.
Manually approach the surface with the cantilever.
Listen to the thermal noise on the raw deflection output from the AFM controller.
As soon as a distinct change in sound is audible, note that the cantilever is within 2-5 µm of the surface.
Enable active feedback on the deflection signal while approaching the surface with the z-piezo.
Stop the approach when the deflection signal increases by a defined amount due to indentation of the surface.
Determine the inverse optical lever sensitivity (InvOLS) by indenting the surface with the cantilever tip.
Use a deflection set point voltage corresponding to a cantilever tip displacement of approximately 3 nm for determining InvOLS.
Fit a simple harmonic oscillator response function to the thermal noise spectrum to determine the spring constant of the cantilever, according to the equipartition theorem.
Initialize an experimental routine with approach speed set at 3,000 nm/sec.
Set the indentation force to 180 pN for measurements.
Set the surface dwell time to 10 msec during measurements.
Retract velocities should be set at 0.2, 0.7, 2.0, and 5.0 µm/sec with corresponding sampling rates of 2,000, 5,000, 15,000, and 20,000 Hz respectively.
Set the retract distance to 500 nm during measurements.
Ensure that the sampling rate is not higher than 10 points/nm to avoid oversampling and keep data sizes reasonable.
Actuate the x- and y-piezo stages to expose a new surface location to the cantilever after each force-distance trace.
Periodically rezero the deflection stage (photodiode position) during long-term measurements.
Adjust the height of the z-piezo chassis if the deflection signal drifts out of range or contact is lost with the surface.
Perform an InvOLS measurement with a significantly higher indentation force at the end of the measurement run to obtain a precise InvOLS value.
Record another thermal noise spectrum far away from the surface after completing the measurements.
Determine the spring constant at the end of the experimental run.
Convert raw signal from the detector into units of force for data analysis.
Correct for offset and drift in the converted data.
Use models of biopolymer elasticity to locate energy barriers in unfolding pathways and identify protein subdomains.
Obtain kinetic and energetic parameters of the receptor-ligand interaction.
Multiply the raw deflection signal by the InvOLS.
Multiply the result of step 1 by the spring constant to convert volts into units of force.
Average the force values from the last 10% of the force-distance trace.
Subtract the average obtained in step 3 from all force values in the data trace.
Offset each trace in the x-direction such that the first intercept with the distance axis occurs at a distance of 0 nm.
Measure the RMS deflection value (noise level under zero force) of the last 10% of each force-distance trace.
Plot the noise vs. curve number and apply an exponential fit or linear fit as appropriate.
Determine a scaling factor for each curve based on the fit parameters obtained in step 7.
Perform deflection correction to transform the distance axis (z) to molecular extension (z*).
Plot the transformed data points in a force vs. contour length plot.
Apply a force threshold of approximately 10 pN to exclude noise.
Exclude unspecific interactions by applying a long-pass length filter.
Assemble a histogram of contour lengths.
Cross-correlate the obtained histograms with a template histogram.
Offset along the x-axis to correct for PEG polydispersity.
Use the resulting correlation values to measure similarity of individual data traces.
Sort traces manually to investigate other unfolding events.
Extract kinetic and energetic information about receptor-ligand dissociation by applying suitable models to the force spectrum.
For a given pulling speed, determine the rupture force for rupture events of interest.
Determine the loading rate from the slope of the line fit to the peak near the rupture event.
Repeat this procedure for every trace showing the rupture event of interest.
Determine the most probable rupture force by applying a Gaussian fit to a histogram of the rupture forces.
Determine the most probable loading rate.
Repeat steps for all pulling speeds.
Plot the most probable rupture forces against the natural logarithm of the most probable loading rates to obtain the force spectrum.
Apply a suitable theoretical model to the force spectrum to extract kinetic and energetic parameters.
